chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from a number of our companions from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ali ibn Hadid from Jamil from one of them from one of the two Imams (peace be upon them):

Regarding a man who bought a sacrificial animal (hady) and slaughtered it, and a man passed by it and recognized it, and said: 'This is my she-camel that went astray from me yesterday,' and two men testified to that for him. He (the Imam) said: 'The meat belongs to him, and it does not count for either of them.' Then he said: 'And for this reason, the Sunnah has been established regarding marking it and tying a ring in its nose if it is identified.'

And the sacrificial animal (hady), if it gives birth, the ruling of its offspring is the ruling of its mother, in that it is obligatory to slaughter both of them together. And there is no harm in benefiting from riding it and drinking its milk, as long as it does not harm it. He narrated.

key_terms.إِشْعَارٌ: Marking the ears of an animal
key_terms.تَقْلِيدٌ: Tying a ring in the nose of a camel
key_terms.هَدْيٌ: A sacrificial animal offered during Hajj or Umrah

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a sacrificial animal recognized by its owner after slaughter?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the jurisprudence of *hady* (sacrificial animal) ownership disputes, establishing that if an animal is recognized by its original owner after purchase and slaughter, the meat belongs to the owner but the sacrifice is not valid for either party. It further details the practical Sunnah of marking the animal (ear notching and nose ring) upon identification and rules that if the animal gives birth, both mother and offspring must be slaughtered, though they can be used for riding and milk before slaughter.
